transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Well, it’s mostly these little mistakes I keep making, and they’re starting to bother me. Like I’ll write down the wrong time on the senior-center class sheet, even though I looked right at it. Or I’ll be working on something at home—wood, a board or whatever—and I measure it once, think I’ve got it, then cut it just a hair short because I skipped over some small print or detail.

It sounds small when I say it out loud, but it keeps happening. And, you know, at the center they’ve got those flyers with tiny type all over them, which doesn’t help, but still… I feel like I should be catching this stuff.
When you make these mistakes, is it usually because you have trouble actually seeing or reading the small print clearly, or do you feel like you saw it fine but your mind just didn't register it?

I think I see it fine, mostly. I mean, I wear my glasses when I need to, and the print on those senior-center flyers is tiny, they really cram everything on there—like the pottery class and the lunch menu all on one sheet—but it’s more like my eyes pass over it and my brain just grabs the wrong thing.

Same with the board I was cutting. I measured it, I looked at the mark, and then somehow I skip one little detail and it’s just a hair short. So it’s not so much that I can’t read it, it’s that I don’t seem to register the small bit I needed.
Have you noticed this kind of forgetfulness and missing small details your whole life, or is this something that's really only started happening in the last months or years?

No, I think it goes way back, honestly. I was actually just looking through some old papers my sister had saved—well, she saves everything, birthday cards from 1980, that kind of thing—and there were these old school comments.

Even in elementary school, teachers would write that I was bright, but I’d forget my books or lose homework, and I’d be staring out the window unless somebody kept me on track. So… it’s not brand new. The mistakes lately bother me more, but that pattern’s been around a long time.

Aside from the attention and memory issues, have you ever noticed a tendency to feel restless, fidgety, or act impulsively—like interrupting others or having trouble sitting still—either now or earlier in your life?

Yeah, I guess restless more than impulsive, if that makes sense. Like sitting through a whole meeting at the senior center—or even just a quiet evening at the condo—I’ll get this ants-in-my-pants feeling. I start thinking I should get up and check something, or straighten something, or putter around in the kitchen.

It’s not like I’m trying to be rude. I just get uncomfortable sitting there too long. I’ll tell myself, “Just stay put,” but then I’m halfway up looking for something that probably didn’t need looking for.

Would you say these attention slips and restlessness have actually caused real problems—like conflicts, missed responsibilities, or trouble keeping up—in more than one area of your life, such as at home, at the senior center, and in your social activities?

Yeah… I’d say it has caused some real problems, though not like everything’s falling apart. More like it makes me less reliable than I want to be.

At the senior center, I’ve kind of stepped back from helping lead a couple of the DIY workshops. I used to enjoy that—showing people how to measure or cut things, you know, and one fellow made this little birdhouse that was actually better than mine—but after a few mix-ups I got worried I’d give the wrong instruction or miss a step.

And at home, my wife has started double-checking plans with me. Like if we’ve got family coming over or something going on at the center, she’ll go over the time or what we’re supposed to bring, because I can throw the whole thing off if I get one detail wrong. I don’t love that, but it’s probably helped.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversation, blurting out answers before someone finishes a question, or having trouble waiting your turn in line or in group settings?

I’m not really sure on that one. I don’t think I’m usually the person jumping in over everybody, at least not that I notice.

Lines, I mean… nobody likes waiting in line. The grocery store near us always seems to have one checkout open when everyone shows up at once, and then I start looking at the magazines or whatever’s by the register. But I don’t think I’m cutting in or causing a problem.

In conversations, maybe I’ll lose the thread sometimes, but blurting out answers before someone’s done… I don’t know. My wife might have a better read on that than I do.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others expect, or feeling like you just can't stay seated for long stretches—like during a movie, church service, or long car ride?

Talking too much… I don’t think that’s the main thing with me. I mean, my wife might say I can get going on a story if it’s about fixing something around the condo—like the time I tried to replace a cabinet hinge and somehow made the door worse—but no, I don’t think I’m usually talking over people.

The sitting still part, though, yes. If I’m in a long meeting, or even just a quiet evening at home, I get this ants-in-my-pants feeling. Like I should get up and check something, or straighten something, or wander into the kitchen and putter around. It’s not dramatic, but sitting there too long starts to feel uncomfortable.
Do you often find yourself making decisions or starting tasks quickly, without waiting to think things through or without waiting for others to finish giving instructions?

Hmm… I’m not sure. I don’t think I’m especially quick to make decisions like that. I mean, if it’s something small, like where to put a shelf or which screwdriver I need, I might just start fiddling with it before I’ve really laid it all out—but I don’t know if that’s what you mean.

With instructions… sometimes I have to stop and think, “Wait, did they finish telling me?” But I wouldn’t say I’m always jumping ahead on purpose. It’s more… I get going, then realize maybe I should’ve listened a little longer. But I’m not sure how often that happens, honestly.
